bibliographic.title: From companion technologies to social care infrastructure: A multi-level perspective on loneliness-related support in dementia care in an era of artificial intelligence (AI)
bibliographic.citation_apa: Uenishi, M., & Song, P. (2026). From companion technologies to social care infrastructure: A multi-level perspective on loneliness-related support in dementia care in an era of artificial intelligence (AI). Global Health & Medicine. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.35772/ghm.2026.01063

methodology.method_family: perspective article proposing a conceptual framework (MCST model) with narrative literature synthesis
methodology.technology_context: companion technologies in dementia care, including socially assistive robots, humanoid and conversational robots, avatars, virtual agents, AI-enabled companions, and LLM-based companion technologies

eligibility.decision_rationale: Perspective article in regulated dementia-care healthcare that explicitly groups LLM-based companion technologies among conversational/AI-enabled systems and discusses ethical governance, human oversight, accountability, audit logs, and escalation. Primary focus is loneliness-related psychosocial support and the MCST care-infrastructure model, not conversational governance of LLMs as the central object of study; authors state dementia-specific evidence for generative AI and LLMs remains insufficient.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: Extracted metadata year (2021) conflicts with DOI/advance publication (2026); only partial PDF text provided; confirm full governance sections and whether article is peer-reviewed.

appraisal.notes: Appropriate as a perspective/framework contribution rather than empirical study. No sample or primary data collection reported in provided text. Governance recommendations for AI-enabled/LLM companions are conceptually argued and supported by cited literature, but LLM-specific effectiveness evidence is explicitly described as preliminary/insufficient.

cerqual.explanation: The MCST model and governance arguments are internally coherent and relevant to regulated healthcare conversational AI, but the provided text is a non-empirical perspective with limited direct LLM evidence and incomplete full-text coverage for adjudication.

axial_codes: risk and safeguard design for conversational AI
coding.theme: Positioning conversational and AI-enabled companion technologies as components of regulated social care infrastructure rather than standalone loneliness interventions
coding.subtheme: Ethical governance and operational safeguards for AI-enabled and LLM-based companions in dementia care

synthesis.main_claim: Companion technologies, including conversational robots and LLM-based companions, should be treated as potential components of social care infrastructure for loneliness-related support in dementia care, with benefits produced through interaction among technology, human facilitation, care workflows, ethical governance, and feedback-based adjustment.
synthesis.contribution: Proposes the MCST three-layer model and argues for evaluation frameworks and practical safeguards—especially human oversight, accountability, audit logs, conversation review, and escalation—for AI-enabled and LLM-based companions in dementia care.
synthesis.limitations: Authors state current dementia-specific evidence for generative AI and large language models is still insufficient and should be presented as a future direction requiring validation, not established effectiveness.
synthesis.use_in_review: Use as supporting conceptual evidence on governance-oriented integration of conversational/LLM companions in regulated healthcare; not suitable as central empirical evidence on conversational governance mechanisms or LLM system operation.

evidence.claim: Article is a perspective proposing the MCST model for loneliness-related support in dementia care using companion technologies and AI.
evidence.excerpt: We propose the multi-level care with social technologies (MCST) model, which consists of three connected layers: individual engagement, relational interaction, and the care ecosystem.

evidence.claim: LLM-based companion technologies are explicitly included among companion technology categories.
evidence.excerpt: We group companion technologies into four broad categories: animal-like socially assistive robots, humanoid robots, conversational robots, and AI-enabled or large language model (LLM)-based companion technologies.

evidence.claim: Dementia-specific evidence for generative AI and LLMs is insufficient.
